newsitem.title: UK: Ireland's Spring sees UK poll as spur to N.I. peace.
newsitem.headline: Ireland's Spring sees UK poll as spur to N.I. peace.

text.p: Irish Deputy Prime Minister Dick Spring on Saturday called on radical nationalist party Sinn Fein and all sides in the Northern Ireland conflict to step up peace efforts after a British election that installed a new government in London.

Spring, a key figure in a stalled Anglo-Irish peace drive, urged two Sinn Fein leaders who won seats in the British parliament in Thursday's election to press their Irish Republican Army (IRA) allies to end violence and pave the way for all-party talks in the British-ruled province.

Gerry Adams and Martin McGuinness gave the IRA's political arm its biggest triumph in more than 40 years by taking Northern Ireland seats in polls that swept Labour to power in Britain for the first time in 18 years.

Speaking on BBC radio, Spring pledged that the Irish Republic would work closely with Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair to end the guerrilla violence and political wrangling that have plagued Northern Ireland's peace hopes.
"There is...a huge onus on the newly-elected MPs. We must have a stop to the violence, we must get them into discussions.
"But the first requirement for everybody now -- and there's some hope, I believe, today -- is to have a ceasefire and to allow everybody into talks," Spring said.
"We have paramilitary violence, confrontational marches, church burnings, sectarian tensions and political intransigence.
"We must get to grips with these things and we will be saying hopefully, if we meet Tony Blair next week, that we want to work with him and work with him immediately to get to grips with these."

Sinn Fein leader Adams, elected in his minority Roman Catholic stronghold of West Belfast, said after his win that it was a message from his backers that Sinn Fein -- so far barred from peace negotiations -- should be given a seat in all-party talks.

Mo Mowlam, the woman likely to become Britain's new Northern Ireland Secretary, has said she would not reverse the stance of her Conservative predecessor that the IRA must call a truce as Sinn Fein's ticket into talks.
Irish newspaper reports said the election of Sinn Fein president Adams, and chief negotiator McGuinness, and Labour's landslide victory, strengthened hopes for a fresh IRA ceasefire.
"The coming weeks could prove crucial in laying the basis for a restored ceasefire with confidence-building measures from both sides (Britain and IRA)," said Dublin's Irish Times.

Belfast's daily nationalist newspaper, The Irish News, said that behind-the-scenes moves would soon be made "to bring key politial players back into action in Washington, London, Dublin and Belfast to try to rebuild the shattered peace process."

Sinn Fein, which increased its overall vote share to 16 per cent in the province-wide election for 18 seats, has been shunned by governments since the IRA reignited violence last year in its 28-year campaign to force an end to British rule.
